{"id": "26:78/q04", "question": "How does the فاء relate creation to guidance?", "turns_on": "Whether the فاء expresses causal sequence, simple coordination, a conditional predicate, or an allowed extra predicate marker; and how الذي is parsed.", "positions": [{"id": "26:78/q04/p1", "position": "The فاء makes guidance follow from creation as its consequence, response or immediate next act.", "reasons": "The author of al-Naẓm contrasts فاء with a mere wāw; al-Bayḍāwī calls it causal if الذي is a subject. Al-Burhān calls guidance the answer to creation; Bursawī says the فاء and present mark renewal. Ibn ʿĀshūr says created intellect makes guidance possible, citing 20:50; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī says gradual bodily creation and governance cannot separate; al-Islāḥī argues leaving a created human to wander would violate mercy and wisdom and make creation futile and unjust. Al-Sāmarrāʾī contrasts immediate فاء here with delayed ثم between death and resurrection. Ālūsī reports the view that creation causes guidance through divine wisdom."}, {"id": "26:78/q04/p2", "position": "The فاء is conjunctive, linking creation and guidance without asserting that creation causes guidance.", "reasons": "Al-Bayḍāwī gives this if the relative modifies رب العالمين; creation is complete while guidance continues."}, {"id": "26:78/q04/p3", "position": "The فاء is licensed by conditional force in the relative subject.", "reasons": "Al-Ḥawfī, followed possibly by Abū al-Baqāʾ, and those reported by Ālūsī use this syntax. Abū Ḥayyān and al-Samīn object that الذي is specific and the creation clause is not renewed. Ālūsī reports al-Rāzī's reply that a general relative is customary but not mandatory; another reply treats creation abstractly as recurring."}, {"id": "26:78/q04/p4", "position": "The فاء may be an added predicate فاء without conditional force.", "reasons": "Al-Samīn says al-Akhfash allows this generally, with the example Zayd fa-ḍribhu; Ālūsī reports the same explanation. Al-Samīn says it could be Abū al-Baqāʾ's unstated basis."}]}
{"id": "26:78/q05", "question": "What does the explicit هو contribute?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "26:78/q05/p1", "position": "It restricts guidance to God alone, answering the idolaters' claim that their gods guide.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr says fronting هو before the verbal predicate gives this restriction and denies that it is a pronoun of separation after a conjunction. {"id": "26:78/q06", "question": "Why is creation past tense and guidance present tense?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "26:78/q06/p1", "position": "Creation was completed once; guidance is renewed and continuous.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī contrasts one creation with recurrent worldly and religious direction; al-Biqāʿī says creation does not recur in this world. Al-Bayḍāwī says creation is complete while guidance continues; al-Nasafī's future-oriented gloss suggests guidance toward what is most necessary, best and most complete."}]}

{"id": "26:78/q08", "question": "Why does Abraham cite these acts of God?", "turns_on": "Whether the focus is the obligation to worship the sole benefactor or the range and sequence of the benefits displayed; several notes make both points.", "positions": [{"id": "26:78/q08/p1", "position": "The acts show that only their divine performer deserves worship and obedience, excluding idols.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī and al-Qurṭubī say the benefactor must be obeyed; al-Māwardī notes creation and guidance are common to all yet Abraham models that duty. Al-Ṭabrisī, Ibn al-Jawzī, al-Rāzī and Study Quran make divinity depend on the listed acts. Ibn ʿAṭiyya calls the human-relevant actions courteous and intelligible, all from God; al-Biqāʿī says the Creator alone knows and rules the creature's inward state and can benefit or harm. Ālūsī reports that special blessings warrant sole worship and reliance. Al-Islāḥī contrasts the source of blessings with deaf, blind, powerless stone idols; Kuran Yolu lists creation, guidance, provision, healing, death, life and forgiveness against fabricated gods. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī rejects treating creation as an insignificant new passage: creation implies divine governance; Ibn ʿĀshūr compares Abraham's devotion with 6:79."}, {"id": "26:78/q08/p2", "position": "The acts display the scope and order of God's beneficence through bodily, intellectual and final life.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī says creation and guidance supply all benefits and begins four attributes after the Lord of the worlds; al-Jishumī says guidance completes blessings. Ibn ʿĀshūr traces bodily and intellectual creation, food, drink, illness, healing, death and resurrection as gifts, with death recognized as a blessing after reflection and later life as plainly one for its seeker. Ālūsī says the named blessings especially warrant worship and reliance."}]}
{"id": "26:78/q09", "question": "How does Abraham's speech function as preaching?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "26:78/q09/p1", "position": "He uses evident personal divine acts to teach true religion and move idolaters toward faith.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya says human-relevant examples let people understand their Lord; al-Rāzī says Abraham rejected false gods, praised God, then prayed, modelling religious instruction. {"id": "26:78/q10", "question": "Why use attributes and repeated relative clauses here?", "turns_on": "Different notes explain distinct stylistic choices in the descriptive sequence.", "positions": [{"id": "26:78/q10/p1", "position": "Abraham speaks of the Beloved by attribute because intimacy overwhelms direct naming.", "reasons": "Al-Wāsiṭī in al-Sulamī contrasts Abraham's earlier direct call to his Lord, before full absorption in attraction, with this indirect naming."}, {"id": "26:78/q10/p2", "position": "Repeating the relative pronoun emphasizes the possessor of three magnificent divine attributes.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr contrasts repetition with simply coordinating the clauses."}]}
{"id": "26:78/q11", "question": "What is the theological force of attributing guidance to God?", "turns_on": "The notes present divine determination broadly or apply it specifically to spiritual ranks and reliance on causes.", "positions": [{"id": "26:78/q11/p1", "position": "God Himself determines and gives guidance, guiding or misguiding whomever He wills.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathīr says God creates and determines each creature's course and guides it, while guiding some and leading others astray by His will. {"id": "26:79/q12", "question": "Which reported cases illustrate sustenance without ordinary meals?", "turns_on": "The reports describe distinct people, places, lengths of abstinence, and means of sustenance.", "positions": [{"id": "26:79/q12/p1", "position": "Sufyan al-Thawri in Mecca lived from one Sabbath to the next on only a handful of sand inhaled.", "reasons": "Muhammad ibn Kathir al-Abdi reports this in al-Thalabi."}, {"id": "26:79/q12/p2", "position": "Ibrahim ibn Adham ate ash and dirt at a kiln and urged freedom from asking people for their possessions.", "reasons": "Al-Thalabi transmits the visitor's encounter; Ibrahim then warns that speech can bring ruin and faults, urging remembrance while speaking and treating the body as dead while silent."}, {"id": "26:79/q12/p3", "position": "A man discarded his waterskin after hearing that God provides every creature, then drank a cup of Paradise in a dream and lived over twenty years without customary food or drink.", "reasons": "Al-Thalabi relates the report and Anas's statement; the recited provision verse is 11:6."}, {"id": "26:79/q12/p4", "position": "Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Nuʿm ate monthly and, after fifteen days confined by Hajjaj, was found praying.", "reasons": "Ali ibn Qadim reports that he said only those who eat and drink need ablution."}, {"id": "26:79/q12/p5", "position": "After a voice offered Abu Saʿid al-Khazzaz eternal satiety while starving in Tarsus, he had no appetite for years but could eat and drink at will.", "reasons": "Al-Thalabi transmits al-Khazzaz's account."}, {"id": "26:79/q12/p6", "position": "A captive woman escaping toward Aleppo traversed two hundred farsakhs without food, drawing strength when hungry from reciting al-Ikhlas three times.", "reasons": "The woman places the journey in Sayf al-Dawla's time; al-Thalabi records her saying that the recitation restored strength, food, and drink, mentioning 112:1."}]}

{"id": "26:79/q15", "question": "How does Abraham use these divine acts in speaking to his people?", "turns_on": "The notes emphasize either an argument from acknowledged acts or the personal mode of presenting that argument.", "positions": [{"id": "26:79/q15/p1", "position": "The acts known to his audience establish that God alone is Lord and worthy of worship.", "reasons": "Al-Mawardi says Abraham cites agreed favors as proof.
